title: Why Correct Findings Don't Get Fixed
description: Diagnose the organisational reasons an accurate, well-evidenced audit produces no change: findings that outlive the routing infrastructure they'd need to become anyone's actual work, accountability gaps where every individual honestly believes someone else owns the fix, accessibility work that loses a rigged competition against the roadmap when pitched as a separate list instead of scoped into the backlog the team already uses, the difference between real remediation and compliance theatre, and how to find the specific person in an organisation who can actually decide to fund a fix.

title: Working With Design and Engineering
description: Give feedback developers and designers can use, at the point where it's cheap to act on it: fitting accessibility review into a team's process rather than inventing a new ceremony, catching barriers in a design file before anything is built, pairing with a developer on a live fix, tracing many findings back to one shared component so a fix ships once instead of forty times, and building a knowledge trail that survives you leaving the room.

title: Making the Case Internally
description: Argue for accessibility work in the terms the person holding the budget actually uses: legal risk, market reach and the rising cost of a late fix, why leading with an inspiration story usually backfires, which numbers survive scrutiny and which fall apart under one follow-up question, writing for the executive who will forward your message without editing it, and using your own lived experience as evidence without letting it become the entire case.

title: From Project to Practice
description: Design the process changes that stop barriers being built in the first place: threading small accessibility gates through a delivery process that already exists rather than bolting one big phase onto the end, writing acceptance criteria specific enough to actually enforce access, scoping an automated CI check honestly instead of overselling it as full coverage, involving disabled users as paid experts rather than simulating disability internally, and diagnosing a team's real maturity stage so the next step is achievable instead of aspirational.
